clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant keratinopathic ichthyosis caused by mutations in KRT2 (keratin 2), which is expressed in the upper spinous and granular layers of the epidermis.
Milder than epidermolytic ichthyosis (KRT1/KRT10), with little or no accompanying erythroderma.
Superficial blistering and erosions occur from birth and with friction, reflecting a plane of cleavage high in the epidermis.
The Mauserung (moulting) phenomenon, with circumscribed areas of superficial peeling leaving normal-looking skin ringed by hyperkeratosis, is highly characteristic.
Grey-brown ridged hyperkeratosis characteristically favours the flexures and shins.
The palms and soles are typically spared, because keratin 2 is not expressed in palmoplantar skin.
Histology shows epidermolytic hyperkeratosis confined to the upper epidermis, distinguishing it from epidermolytic ichthyosis where the change is deeper.
Neonatal blistering and erosions carry a risk of secondary infection and fluid loss.
reference.pathophysiology: Ichthyosis bullosa of Siemens is caused by dominant-negative mutations in KRT2, which encodes keratin 2, a type II keratin expressed specifically in the upper spinous and granular layers of the epidermis where it partners with keratin 10. Mutant keratin 2 disrupts assembly of the intermediate filament cytoskeleton in these superficial keratinocytes, producing keratin clumping and cytolysis high in the epidermis. This superficial cytolysis creates fragile, easily denuded skin, superficial blistering and the characteristic moulting (Mauserung) as the abnormal cornified layer sheds to reveal underlying skin. Because keratin 2 is not expressed in the lower epidermis or in palmoplantar skin, the split remains confined to the upper layers and the palms and soles are spared, in contrast to epidermolytic ichthyosis, where mutations in the suprabasal keratins 1 and 10 cause deeper, more widespread cytolysis and erythroderma.
additionalDifferentials: Superficial epidermolytic ichthyosis and acral peeling skin syndrome
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome in the neonate
Other congenital ichthyoses associated with blistering
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing epidermolytic hyperkeratosis limited to the upper epidermis
Molecular genetic testing for KRT2 variants
Electron microscopy demonstrating clumped keratin tonofilaments in upper keratinocytes
Swabs of eroded skin to identify secondary bacterial infection
Detailed family history and examination of relatives given dominant inheritance
Assessment of lesion distribution to confirm palmoplantar sparing
redFlags: Extensive neonatal erosions with a risk of sepsis and fluid or electrolyte loss
Spreading secondary bacterial infection of denuded skin
Rapidly enlarging tender bullae suggesting superadded staphylococcal infection
reference.prognosis: The condition is generally mild and compatible with a normal life expectancy. Blistering tends to lessen after infancy, while hyperkeratosis and the moulting phenomenon persist into adult life.
pitfalls: Confusing it with the more severe epidermolytic ichthyosis; palmoplantar sparing and the superficial split are key discriminators.
Mistaking neonatal blistering for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome or epidermolysis bullosa.
Failing to recognise the Mauserung phenomenon as a diagnostic clue.
Over-treating with systemic agents when topical emollients and keratolytics usually suffice.

management: Reduce scale and hyperkeratosis with regular emollients and keratolytics (urea, lactic acid) as the mainstay of supportive care
Minimise friction and mechanical trauma to limit superficial blistering and erosions
Consider systemic retinoids for troublesome hyperkeratosis under specialist supervision, balancing benefit against skin fragility
Swab and treat secondarily infected eroded skin with appropriate antibiotics
Provide wound care for denuded areas and the moulting (Mauserung) phenomenon
Confirm the diagnosis by KRT2 testing and offer genetic counselling with examination of relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance
